title.value: Things I Learned From the Recent Turkish Earthquake That You Should Be Able to Use in Your Own Work

note.value:
The August 17, Izmit, and November 12, Duzce earthquakes (Mw 7.4 and 7.1, respectively) represent the most recent two of a series of large earthquakes along the North Anatolian Fault, a highly active right-lateral strike-slip fault that crosses the Anatolian Peninsula in Turkey from one end to the other. The first earthquake rupture apparently initiated at a small stepover along a relatively inconspicuous fault strand following the southern coast of the Izmit Bay and propagated to the west and to the east for a distance of 125 to 150 km. The western segment goes into the Bay in both directions after attaining the largest surface slip about 5 m at the town of Golcuk. The eastern extension of the surface rupture associated with the first earthquake is composed of five major segments with the maximum slip magnitudes 3 to 4, 4.5, 0.5, 1.4, and 0.1 m from west to east, respectively. The segment with 0.5 m slip trends N 700 W, the segment with 1.4-m slip trends N 700 E, and the easternmost segment with minor slip trends E-W again.

The surface manifestation of the second earthquake is an extensively segmented rupture trace with dominant transtensional deformation. It has a normal slip component of more than 3.7 m and a right lateral slip close to 1.4 m along the western part which showed minor rupture during the first earthquake. The central part has a transpressional character with about 1-m reverse slip and about 3-m right lateral slip. The highest right lateral slip (nearly 5 m) occurs near the eastern end of the central part. The eastern part of the rupture displays a typical strike-slip deformation with its greatest right lateral slip of about 3 m and minor local vertical slip which exhibits changing polarity.
The varying orientations of the rupture segments reflect the fault mosaic of the broader region and the interaction between neighboring faults. The temporal and spatial characteristics of the rupture segments, as well as the significance of the nearly three months time period between the first and second earthquakes, pose highly challenging mechanical problems regarding the rupture initiation, propagation, and termination processes. The main surface rupture zone, although unusually narrow (2.5 to 6 m), left a path of death and destruction.

This study has several implications for interpretation of strike-slip faults that you can use in your own work related to strike-slip faults: (1) The fault architecture deduced from the surface rupture in alluvium displays a transpressional flower structure in an other- wise transtensional strike-slip environment. This is similar to some surface images of strike slip faults in sedimentary cover, which was driven by basement faults. (2) There appears to be a relationship between the maximum right-lateral surface slip and the segment length, Smax/L= 1 x 10-4 to 2 x 10-4. The normal component of slip is localized at stepovers and areas with the great- est slip gradient. These areas correspond to high concentration of extensional structures such as joints and normal faults and characterize enhanced permeability along the fault. This is evident, at least in one location, by the occurrence of hot springs. (4) Don’t build your house within a fault zone!

Aydin, Atilla. (2000). Things I Learned From the Recent Turkish Earthquake That You Should Be Able to Use in Your Own Work. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/qm861dk8052
